title: Optimization of multiclass queueing networks: Polyhedral and nonlinear characterizations of achievable performance
contribution: Recasts optimal sequencing and routing in multiclass queueing networks as optimization over the achievable performance region. Quadratic and higher-order potential functions in the uniformized Markov chain generate constraints that every policy satisfies: a parametric version with 2^R-1 inequalities, and a dominating nonparametric version with O(R^2) variables and constraints. Jensen-type PSD constraints, separated by SDP, add a nonlinear layer. The first-order polyhedron is exact for Klimov's problem, the multiclass M/M/1 queue and homogeneous networks, with a polynomial-size reformulation of the extended polymatroid. On four small networks the LP bounds certify heuristic policies at 62-99% efficiency.
problem_entry: SD+LO+CP: simulation, the usual way to evaluate policies for multiclass networks (no product form even under FCFS), says nothing about distance from optimality. Entry: transplant discrete optimization's lower bounds, and characterize the achievable region so that the stochastic dynamic problem becomes a mathematical program (pp. 2-3, 6-7).
key_idea: For a potential R = sum f(r) n_r(t), E[R^2] is invariant in the steady state of the uniformized chain, which yields constraints valid for every policy. Freeing the weights and matching coefficients turns one bound into a polyhedron. Higher-degree potentials and Jensen PSD constraints give a hierarchy, exact wherever strong conservation laws hold (pp. 8-26).
assumptions: Open (and closed) networks: Poisson arrivals, exponential class-dependent services, Markovian routing. Policies Markovian, possibly idling and preemptive, with a unique invariant distribution and finite second moments, adopted 'For technical reasons'. Work-conserving policies for the exactness results. Routing, closed networks and phase-type services only outlined. Small synthetic examples; no real data and no owner (pp. 5-6, 10-11, 18-20, 23-31).
proof_devices: steady-state invariance of E[R^2] combined with E[1{B_r}] = lambda_r/mu_r and Little's law; one inequality proved, the rest 'derived similarly' (pp. 8-10)
f-parameter condition (17), which aggregates per-station busy indicators before bounding them by 1; f = expected remaining processing time gives the heavy-traffic denominator (pp. 12-14)
coefficient matching of two quadratic forms in f that agree for all f (Theorem 4.2, p. 16), equivalent to test functions n_r^2 and n_r n_r' (p. 16)
dominance of the nonparametric polyhedron by projection (Theorem 4.3, pp. 17-18)
a stability-based bound (Theorem 3.2, p. 10) and a cut from a cost vector with known optimal policy, the tandem queue (pp. 10-11)
higher-degree potentials giving an O(R^i) hierarchy (p. 20)
Jensen inequality E[Y'QY] >= E[Y]'QE[Y] for all PSD Q, imposed by cutting planes with SDP separation, polynomial via the ellipsoid method or Vaidya's algorithm (pp. 21-22)
exactness: tightness at priority rules plus strong conservation laws plus the Bertsimas-Nino-Mora extended-polymatroid theorem (pp. 24-26)
exact polynomial-size (O(R^2)) reformulation of an extended polymatroid with 2^R-1 constraints (pp. 23, 26)
asymptotic exactness of the routing bound via Foschini-Salz (pp. 29-30)
experiments: Four small synthetic networks: Harrison-Wein 3-class, a 6-class two-station network, two-server routing, a closed 6-class network. Efficiency = lower bound / best policy found (simulated thresholds, priority rules, JSQ, a heavy-traffic policy): 83-96%, 62-95%, 72-92% and 97-99%. The nonparametric bound is strictly better on the 6-class network. No solver, run times or confidence intervals, except Table 7. Higher-order and SDP bounds not computed (pp. 26-32).
positioning: Extends the conservation-law lineage (Gelenbe-Mitrani, Federgruen-Groenevelt, Shanthikumar-Yao, Tsoucas, Bertsimas-Nino-Mora). The Brownian heavy-traffic school is credited but weaker for open networks, and its policies serve as the upper bounds. Ou-Wein's bounds need simulation. Kumar's single weak inequality is generalized, with priority claimed over Kumar-Kumar. SDP ideas are credited to Lovasz-Schrijver and Alizadeh (pp. 3-5, 11, 14, 27, 30).
writing: Four numbered contributions; a toy network first; one inequality proved, the rest deferred to Paschalidis's M.S. thesis; a 'software tool' pitch; hedges ('we believe', 'A plausible explanation'). The abstract says 'at least as good as', the body 'comparable'. A slip on p. 18 swaps the two LPs' sizes. Closes with a one-page 'Reflections' (pp. 1-5, 8, 17-18, 21, 27, 31-32).
limits_future: Best f-parameters unknown; the O(R^i) hierarchy is prohibitive; a gap persists because the region is not always a polyhedron; efficiency only 62% in heavy balanced traffic; higher-order and nonlinear bounds untested; tightness in actual applications unchecked. No policy derived from the relaxations for networks [card-writer's reading]. The SDP layer was computed later in S007 (pp. 14, 20-21, 27-32).

method_links.note: Steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 in SD. The owning practice is named (simulation without an optimality yardstick; heavy-traffic models weaker for open networks); performance vectors are the variables; the class is kept (an O(R^2) LP, then convex constraints with SDP separation); the boundary is printed. No dual reading here (S185 supplies it). It is a [stated-joint] SD methodology that qualifies the Domain Map's 'no stated methodology found'. 'Efficiently' means polynomial time, supporting the note that tractable later drifts to solve time.

The certificate half without an exact solve: the lower bound is the certificate, and the gap is reported as efficiency against the best policy found, with the admission that this upper bound overstates the optimum. The rival school's policies (Harrison-Wein thresholds, heavy-traffic priorities) are certified, not beaten: 83-99% in most regimes, 62% in the worst. No policy is computed from the bound.

Step 3, thesis lineage: the omitted proofs are in Paschalidis's 1992 M.S. thesis, with Tsitsiklis as co-author (SKILL.md lists Paschalidis in the SD lineage). The work went workshop, conference, technical report, journal, funded by the PYI award with Draper matching funds and Leaders for Manufacturing.

The 'why now' is qualitative: new semidefinite relaxation tools from integer programming, and symbolic algebra feeding an LP solver. No figure, and the problem had not been written off as intractable.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Pairwise (quadratic potential) constraints, then i-wise ones from higher-degree potentials, in O(R^i) size, with an explicit accuracy-tractability trade-off; Jensen PSD constraints on top.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: PSD moment-matrix strengthening carried across domains
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: E[Y'QY] >= E[Y]'QE[Y] for every PSD Q on queue-length moment variables, credited to SDP lower bounds in integer programming (Lovasz-Schrijver, Alizadeh); its earliest appearance in the cards so far, before S185 and S007.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bound-referenced quality yardstick for heuristics and policies
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Efficiency = lower bound / best policy found, used to judge FCFS, Harrison-Wein thresholds, priority rules, JSQ and heavy-traffic policies.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: re-derive classical theorems with the new device
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The M/M/1 conservation law, Gelenbe-Mitrani's region, Klimov's region and Ross-Yao recovered from potential functions.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: symbolic-algebra pipeline from model description to bound or policy
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Mathematica or Maple collects the coefficients of polynomial identities into constraints and feeds an LP solver: 'the user provides the data' and receives a lower bound. Also S098 (Maple heuristic with LaTeX output).

transferable: When a field judges policies by simulation alone, enter by supplying the missing yardstick: a bound computed in closed form from the data, offered as a tool (pp. 2-3, 5).

To turn one potential-function inequality into a polyhedron, make the weights free, keep the cross moments as variables, and require the identity for all weights, equating quadratic forms coefficient by coefficient (pp. 15-16).
Choose potential weights so that indicator terms aggregate per station before they are bounded; weights equal to expected remaining processing times recover the heavy-traffic denominator (pp. 13-14).
Collect known-optimum cuts: every cost vector whose optimal policy and cost are known gives a valid inequality on the achievable region (pp. 10-11).
To prove a relaxation exact, show that a specific policy (priority to S) attains each inequality, then invoke a polyhedral characterization theorem (pp. 24-26).
Add Jensen-type PSD constraints on expectations of products to any relaxation whose variables are moments; separate the violated ones by an SDP or an eigenvalue test (pp. 21-22).

Report efficiency as lower bound over best policy found, across a grid of balanced and imbalanced loads; say that the denominator overestimates the optimum, and explain tightness by the exactly solved special case (one bottleneck behaves like one station) (pp. 26-31).
Automate the derivation: symbolic manipulation of polynomial identities generates the constraints, an LP solver computes the bound, and the pipeline is presented as a tool (pp. 17, 21).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis, John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: In the tradition of discrete optimization in the mathematical programming community, we develop a sequence of lower bounds to the optimal cost.
Since the optimal cost is not known, we cannot calculate the closeness of our lower bound to the optimal cost.

title: Fluid models of sequencing problems in open queueing networks; an optimal control approach
contribution: Treats sequencing in open multiclass networks as a deterministic fluid optimal control problem (a linear control problem over a polyhedron). Pontryagin's maximum principle yields dynamic priority indices and explicit threshold policies with linear switching curves for small networks. A time-discretized LP, refined by halving, serves as a numerical yardstick. A 'learning' pairwise-interaction heuristic, implemented in Maple, picks the LP vertex selected by weights fitted to exactly solved two-class building blocks, and it matched the yardstick's time-zero controls on networks of up to nine classes (read as the June 1994 preprint, titled 'An Optimal Control Approach to Optimization of Multiclass Queueing Networks').
problem_entry: SD+LO (HS for the heuristic): the S072 problem, with the difficulty split into dynamic, combinatorial and stochastic parts. A 'philosophical view' drops the stochastic part, since a deterministic dynamic model reveals the policy structure. Starting point: Chen-Yao's fluid model and its myopic LP solution (p. 2); problem (CONTROL) asks for the optimal u(0) as a function of x(0) (pp. 5-6).
key_idea: The optimal control serves the class with the largest dynamic index mu_i(y_i - y_next) from the adjoint multipliers, which foresees downstream depletions. Small networks give explicit threshold policies, e.g. hold station 1 while x1/x2 < (c2/c1)(mu1 - lambda)/(mu2 - mu1). In the heuristic every extreme point of the feasible-velocity polytope is the LP optimum of some weight w, so policies are weights fitted from exact building blocks (pp. 6-8, 11-14, 20-24).
assumptions: Deterministic fluid model: continuous queue contents, control fractions u_i in [0,1] summing to at most 1 per station, given routing, external arrival rates b, a horizon long enough to empty the system. Stochasticity removed by assumption. x(0) > 0 and stability in the examples; b = 0 for the maximum-principle reduction; A nonsingular for the heuristic; Theorem 5 without proof; no data (pp. 2, 5-7, 9, 17, 20).
proof_devices: Pontryagin maximum principle: Hamiltonian, adjoint dy/dt = -c, transversality; a switch requires equal dynamic indices (continuity of H); DEPLETIONS vs INTERRUPTS, with the event order to be guessed (pp. 7-8)
Proposition: cofactors decrease linearly, indices are piecewise linear with at most N_i + 1 slope changes; 'tooth'-shaped indices explain holding (p. 8)
the mu-c rule re-derived from the maximum principle (Theorem 2, p. 10)
threshold by perturbation: closed-form cost of never holding F_N vs holding for small Delta, difference Delta^2 A + Delta B with A > 0, so hold iff B < 0 (pp. 12-14)
reduction of competition at node 1 to a 'modified tandem' with effective costs c1mu1 - c3mu3 and c2mu1 (Theorem 4, p. 16)

time-discretized LP with 2nT/h variables, feasible for the original problem (Pullan) and hence an upper bound; step halving with simplex warm start; stop at under 5% improvement with a binary u(0) (pp. 18-19)
every extreme point of a polyhedron is the unique optimum of some linear objective, giving the policy parametrization w (p. 21)

building-block theorems: w = c reproduces the optimal control for competing classes (Theorem 6, p. 23); a state-dependent w for tandem classes (Theorem 7, pp. 24-25); least-squares combination Mw = 0, w'e = 1 (pp. 21-22)
experiments: The discretized LP reproduces the analytical tandem threshold (Fig. 7). The heuristic is compared with the LP by the time-zero control over grids of initial states: two 4-class networks (threshold found, slope slightly off or identical), a 6-class reentrant line (identical), and the 9-class Kumar-Perkins network (two instances only, identical). No costs, run times or solver reported; the myopic Chen-Yao rule is not run. Claims of 'hundreds of classes' and 'large scale problems' exceed the nine classes shown (pp. 3, 20, 28-30, 33).
positioning: Builds on Chen-Yao's fluid model and replaces their myopic LP sequence with explicit threshold policies; cites optimal control of communication fluid models and characterizes Harrison-Wein's Brownian threshold explicitly. Lower bounds left to Ou-Wein and Bertsimas-Paschalidis-Tsitsiklis. Infinite LP via the SCLP literature (Anderson, Anderson-Nash, Pullan). The introduction and the Brownian-models paragraph reuse S072's text almost verbatim (pp. 2-3, 18; S072 pp. 2, 4-5).
writing: A stated 'philosophical view' up front, returned to after the mu-c example; three numbered contributions. Speed and scale claims without timings ('very fast and completely automatic', 'extremely fast', 'extensive computational results'); 'optimal' and 'exactly' used for a discretization stopped at 5% improvement. Draft marks: '[?]' citations, a mismatched roadmap, a missing appendix, typos. Candid notes on what is not implemented; a conjecture-led close (pp. 1-4, 8, 10, 19, 22, 28, 33).
limits_future: Exact method limited to about ten stations, and an optimal algorithm is open (taken up by S156); the heuristic misses slopes; learning and three-way interactions not implemented; symbolic output needs manual simplification; the stochastic layer is untested. Conjecture: stochastic threshold curves are higher-order curves with qualitatively unchanged policies. Policies are never evaluated in a stochastic network [card-writer's reading] (pp. 3, 22, 28-29, 33).

method_links.note: SD to LO: a stochastic control problem becomes a deterministic linear control problem (an infinite LP or SCLP), solved as a finite LP after discretization; structure is read off the adjoint multipliers (dynamic indices), the analogue of step 4; the boundary is printed (about ten stations, no optimal algorithm). Departure: the class is reached through a relaxation (the fluid model), not an exact reformulation, and the link back to the stochastic problem is conjectured. Tension T3: a [stated-joint] 1994 statement of the optimization pole for SD.

An exact-solve yardstick judges a fast heuristic, but the incumbent (Chen-Yao's myopic rule) is analysed, not run. The 'exact' LP is a discretization stopped at under 5% improvement yet called optimal (an early Tension T1), and the comparison covers the time-zero control, not cost. Tension T6: 'hundreds of classes' against nine shown.

Step 3: a cohort work with an MIT ORC co-author (Ricard) and a repeat collaborator (Avram), listed in the 1995 survey S185, PYI-funded with Draper matching funds. Its open problem, an optimal algorithm, becomes the next student paper (S156, which cites Avram-Bertsimas-Ricard).
method_links.pages: preprint pp. 1, 33; card S185 p. 4; card S156 p. 2

method_links.note: Step 6 only, seen across cards: the 1994 special-case threshold policies, whose curves 'are hyperplanes' in the fluid model, are taken up again under the ML lens in S402, which generalizes Avram et al. (1995) and learns the policy with OCT-H. S098 itself makes no quantified 'why now'.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Stated philosophical view that the dynamic and combinatorial parts reveal the structure of optimal policies, supported by the mu-c rule (optimal in both models); the stochastic effect is left as a conjecture (thresholds become higher-order curves, policies qualitatively unchanged).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: learn a policy from exactly solved small motifs
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Building blocks (competing classes, tandem classes) solved exactly by the maximum principle fix the weight ratios of an LP-vertex policy for larger networks; more exactly solved networks would add equations ('learning from special cases'). A 1994 precursor of SKILL Heuristic 5, learning from small exact cases instead of data.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: S072 gives lower bounds and S098 gives policies for the same open multiclass sequencing problem, sharing an introduction; S007 later pairs fluid-control policies with SDP bounds.

transferable: Name the components of a problem's difficulty, say which one you drop and why, and test the stance on a case where the answer is known (the mu-c rule) (pp. 2, 10).

Parametrize a policy as the LP vertex that weight vector w picks over the polytope of feasible velocities; fit w so that the policy reproduces exact solutions of small subsystems, and combine them by least squares (pp. 20-24).
To locate a switching curve, compare the closed-form cost of acting now with that of waiting Delta and then acting; the sign of the term linear in Delta gives the threshold (pp. 12-14).
Reduce a new network to a solved one through effective costs: competition at node 1 becomes a 'modified tandem' (p. 16).
Refine a time discretization by halving, warm-start each LP from the coarse solution (which stays feasible), stop on a stated relative-improvement rule, and report the rule (p. 19).
Compare a heuristic with the exact solution as a policy map over a grid of initial states, which shows whether the switching curve exists and how far its slope is off (pp. 20, 28-29).

quotes.text: In other words, while the stochastic component of the problem is important, the structure of the optimal policies can be revealed by a deterministic and dynamic model.
Philosophically the heuristic attacks the general problem by learning from special cases.
